lion-tail.sourceRecipe: Smuggler's Cove spec (Jamaican rum, allspice dram, lime)
lion-tail.recipeProvenance: Modern tiki canon documenting Jamaican bar culture.
lion-tail.historicalNotes: Named for the Lion's Tail tavern legend in Kingston; the allspice dram marks it as a Jamaican cousin to the sour template.
lion-tail.funFact: Allspice dram turns a plain bourbon sour into something that smells like Kingston spice markets—one of the few classics built around pimento liqueur.
lion-tail.sourceAttribution: Smuggler's Cove — Martin Cate & Rebecca Cate

corn-and-oil.sourceRecipe: Smuggler's Cove Corn 'n' Oil (blackstrap, falernum, lime)
corn-and-oil.recipeProvenance: Barbados highball documented in modern tiki scholarship.
corn-and-oil.historicalNotes: Barbados' everyday rum highball—falernum and blackstrap on ice predates the tiki movement but anchors Caribbean rum culture.
corn-and-oil.funFact: Barbados bartenders treat this like a beer: blackstrap rum, falernum, and a spent lime shell on ice—no shaker required.
corn-and-oil.sourceAttribution: Smuggler's Cove — Martin Cate & Rebecca Cate

airmail.historicalNotes: Craddock's Airmail reads like a Daiquiri lengthened with bubbly—named for the romance of early aviation mail routes.
airmail.funFact: Harry Craddock floated champagne on a honeyed rum sour and called it Airmail—1930s marketing for the dawn of transatlantic flight.
airmail.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

taboo.recipeProvenance: Tiki historian spec from lost Donn Beach notes.
taboo.historicalNotes: Don the Beachcomber's lost-book recipe Berry calls Taboo—distinct from the later passion-fruit tiki slug already in CRAFT as taboo-tiki.
taboo.funFact: Jeff Berry dug this name out of Donn Beach's cryptic notebooks—a banana-and-coconut blend separate from the passion-fruit Taboo already in the expanded set.

donn-beach-grog.recipeProvenance: Reconstructed from Don the Beachcomber recipe logs.
donn-beach-grog.historicalNotes: One of Donn Beach's early grogs served at the Hollywood Beachcomber—rum, citrus, and spice built for long afternoons.
donn-beach-grog.creator: Donn Beach
donn-beach-grog.funFact: Before the Zombie made Donn Beach famous, grogs like this one trained Hollywood regulars to expect rum served like a meal.

eastern-standard.sourceAuthor: David Kaplan, Nick Fauchald, Alex Day
eastern-standard.sourceRecipe: Death & Co Eastern Standard (bourbon, mint, lime, sugar)
eastern-standard.historicalNotes: A bourbon Southside—mint and lime soften the whiskey for a bar snack-friendly sipper born in New York's neo-speakeasy era.
eastern-standard.creator: Phil Ward
eastern-standard.funFact: Death & Co framed this as a bourbon Southside: mint bruised with lime and simple syrup so the whiskey reads bright, not boozy.
eastern-standard.sourceAttribution: Death & Co — David Kaplan, Nick Fauchald, Alex Day

hotel-nacional.sourceRecipe: Savoy Hotel Nacional Special (rum, pineapple, lime, apricot)
hotel-nacional.historicalNotes: Named for Havana's Hotel Nacional—pineapple and apricot liqueur wrap around Cuban rum in a pre-revolution luxury hotel template.
hotel-nacional.funFact: Havana's Hotel Nacional lent its name to this pineapple-apricot rum sour long before American tourists discovered the mojito.
hotel-nacional.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

pimm-cup.sourceRecipe: Classic Pimm's Cup (No. 1, lemon, cucumber, lemonade)
pimm-cup.recipeProvenance: British pub and tennis standard since mid-1800s.
pimm-cup.historicalNotes: James Pimm sold the tonic cup at his London oyster house; cucumber and effervescence made it the default English summer drink.
pimm-cup.creator: James Pimm
pimm-cup.funFact: Wimbledon pours thousands of these each year—Pimm's No. 1 was originally marketed as a digestive tonic, not a lawn party prop.

paradise.sourceRecipe: IBA Paradise (gin, apricot brandy, orange juice)
paradise.historicalNotes: A two-ingredient gin sling lengthened with orange—post-war IBA canon showcasing apricot brandy in a simple sour family drink.
paradise.funFact: The IBA Paradise is barely a recipe—gin, apricot brandy, and orange juice—but that simplicity made it a hotel-bar staple across Europe.
paradise.sourceAttribution: IBA Official Cocktails — International Bartenders Association

yellow-bird.sourceRecipe: IBA Yellow Bird (rum, Galliano, triple sec, lime)
yellow-bird.historicalNotes: Jamaican rum meets Galliano's vanilla anise in a shaken sour—1960s international hotel culture in one glass.
yellow-bird.funFact: Galliano's tall vanilla profile makes the Yellow Bird taste sweeter than the spec suggests—shake hard to keep lime in balance.
yellow-bird.sourceAttribution: IBA Official Cocktails — International Bartenders Association

flamingo.historicalNotes: Apricot brandy and white rum form a twin-spirit sour—the Flamingo name nods to pink-hued hotel-bar glamour of the mid-century.
flamingo.funFact: White rum plus apricot brandy yields a blush-pink sour without grenadine—the IBA spec keeps the fruit flavor dry and spirit-forward.
flamingo.sourceAttribution: IBA Official Cocktails — International Bartenders Association

deauville.historicalNotes: Normandy apple brandy shaken with citrus and orange liqueur—Craddock's tribute to the Deauville resort crowd.
deauville.funFact: Calvados replaces gin in a sour skeleton here—Craddock wrote it for travelers who wanted Normandy in a coupe.
deauville.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

dubonnet-cocktail.historicalNotes: Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother favored gin with Dubonnet—Craddock codified the two-ingredient stir in the Savoy.
dubonnet-cocktail.funFact: The late Queen Mother drank gin and Dubonnet daily before lunch—this two-part stir is royal habit turned bar standard.
dubonnet-cocktail.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

morning-glory-fizz.sourceRecipe: Morning Glory Fizz (scotch, egg white, citrus, soda, absinthe rinse)
morning-glory-fizz.historicalNotes: A bracing hair-of-the-dog fizz—scotch, whole egg, dual citrus, and absinthe made it a Gilded Age morning ritual.
morning-glory-fizz.funFact: Bartenders shook this fizz at dawn for weary revelers—absinthe rinse and scotch in the same glass was Victorian audacity.
morning-glory-fizz.sourceAttribution: How to Mix Drinks — Jerry Thomas

purgatory.sourceRecipe: Death & Co Purgatory (rye, green Chartreuse, dry vermouth)
purgatory.historicalNotes: Chartreuse and rye in equal tension—Death & Co's name signals a Last Word cousin built for Manhattan whiskey drinkers.
purgatory.funFact: Green Chartreuse and rye share herbal weight—this stirred trio drinks like a whiskey Last Word with dry vermouth softening the finish.
purgatory.sourceAttribution: Death & Co — David Kaplan et al.

satan-whiskers.historicalNotes: Orange juice in a vermouth-gin split—Craddock offered 'straight' and 'curled' variants with Grand Marnier versus orange bitters.
satan-whiskers.funFact: Craddock printed Satan's Whiskers two ways—Grand Marnier makes it 'Straight,' orange bitters make it 'Curled'—same cheeky name either path.
satan-whiskers.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

vermouth-cassiss.sourceRecipe: Savoy Vermouth Cassis (dry vermouth, crème de cassis)
vermouth-cassiss.historicalNotes: A French aperitif template—dry vermouth lengthened with blackcurrant liqueur before the Kir popularized wine-based versions.
vermouth-cassiss.funFact: Before the Kir switched to still wine, bartenders built this on dry vermouth—blackcurrant sweetness against herbal dry wine.
vermouth-cassiss.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

whiskey-rickey.historicalNotes: Colonel Rickey's Washington DC order became the template—spirit, lime, soda, no sugar in the original whiskey version.
whiskey-rickey.funFact: The Rickey predates the Moscow Mule's vodka swap by decades—lime and soda over whiskey was Washington DC's summer default.
whiskey-rickey.sourceAttribution: How to Mix Drinks — Jerry Thomas

charleston.historicalNotes: Bitters and grenadine tint a rum sour—1920s American name evoking Jazz Age South Carolina glamour.
charleston.funFact: A few dashes of Angostura and grenadine turn a plain rum sour pink—IBA keeps the spec deliberately small.
charleston.sourceAttribution: IBA Official Cocktails — International Bartenders Association

harvard.historicalNotes: Named for Harvard University—cognac and Italian vermouth topped with soda in a gentler Manhattan highball.
harvard.funFact: Craddock's Harvard splits the difference between a Manhattan and a highball—soda keeps the cognac sessionable.
harvard.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

horse-neck.sourceRecipe: Savoy Horse's Neck (bourbon, ginger ale, lemon peel)
horse-neck.historicalNotes: A long lemon peel spirals over ginger ale and bourbon—the garnish shape gives the drink its equestrian name.
horse-neck.funFact: The Horse's Neck is mostly garnish theater: one long lemon spiral draped over ginger ale and bourbon in a highball.
horse-neck.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

kir.sourceRecipe: IBA Kir (white wine, crème de cassis)
kir.historicalNotes: Canon Félix Kir popularized crème de cassis with Aligoté—white wine replaced vermouth in post-war French aperitivo culture.
kir.creator: Félix Kir
kir.funFact: Mayor Canon Kir lent his name to blackcurrant wine after WWII—every French bistro still pours the template.
kir.sourceAttribution: IBA Official Cocktails — International Bartenders Association

palmetto.historicalNotes: Rum replaces whiskey in a split-vermouth Manhattan—named for South Carolina's Palmetto state symbol.
palmetto.funFact: Split sweet and dry vermouth with aged rum drinks like a tropical Manhattan without leaving the coupe format.
palmetto.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

coffee-cocktail.historicalNotes: Named for its coffee-like appearance—port and cognac shaken with egg yolk mimic a latte cap despite zero caffeine.
coffee-cocktail.funFact: Thomas's Coffee Cocktail never saw coffee beans—the name describes the foamy tan head from port, brandy, and egg.
coffee-cocktail.sourceAttribution: How to Mix Drinks — Jerry Thomas

blue-blazer.sourceRecipe: Blue Blazer (scotch, hot water, sugar, flaming toss)
blue-blazer.historicalNotes: Thomas tossed flaming scotch between mugs—performed for audiences rather than everyday service.
blue-blazer.creator: Jerry Thomas
blue-blazer.funFact: Jerry Thomas lit scotch on fire and poured it between two mugs in an arc—the original flair bartending stunt.
blue-blazer.sourceAttribution: How to Mix Drinks — Jerry Thomas

brandy-flip.historicalNotes: Whole egg and sugar enrich brandy in the flip template that predates cream liqueurs by a century.
brandy-flip.funFact: Flips once used hot pokers to froth ale—by Thomas's era brandy, egg, and nutmeg did the job shaken cold.
brandy-flip.sourceAttribution: How to Mix Drinks — Jerry Thomas

cooperstown.sourceRecipe: Savoy Cooperstown (gin, dry vermouth, mint, orange bitters)
cooperstown.historicalNotes: Named for the New York baseball town—mint and orange bitters lift a dry Martini structure.
cooperstown.funFact: Craddock added mint to a fifty-fifty Martini and named it for Cooperstown—baseball's hall of fame in a glass.
cooperstown.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

chicago-fizz.sourceRecipe: Savoy Chicago Fizz (rum, port, citrus, egg white, soda)
chicago-fizz.historicalNotes: Port and rum share the base with a split citrus fizz—Chicago's pre-Prohibition bar culture in a Collins glass.
chicago-fizz.funFact: Port in a fizz is rare today—Craddock's Chicago version splits rum and ruby port before the soda top.
chicago-fizz.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

artillery.historicalNotes: Sweet vermouth leads with gin as modifier—named for the punch of its fortified wine base.
artillery.funFact: Reverse the Manhattan ratios and you get Artillery—vermouth-heavy, gin as seasoning.
artillery.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

ford-cocktail.sourceRecipe: Savoy Ford Cocktail (gin, dry vermouth, Benedictine)
ford-cocktail.historicalNotes: A dry Martini sweetened with Benedictine—named for automotive pioneer Henry Ford's era.
ford-cocktail.funFact: One barspoon of Benedictine turns a dry Martini into the Ford—herbal honey without full sweetness.
ford-cocktail.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

golden-cadillac.sourceRecipe: Golden Cadillac (Galliano, crème de cacao, cream)
golden-cadillac.historicalNotes: Invented after a Cadillac purchase at Los Angeles' Poor Red's—Galliano and white cacao define the after-dinner sipper.
golden-cadillac.funFact: Poor Red's in California claims a newly purchased Cadillac inspired this cream-and-Galliano dessert drink in 1952.
golden-cadillac.sourceAttribution: The Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book — Albert Stevens Crockett

metropole.sourceRecipe: Savoy Metropole (cognac, dry vermouth, syrup, bitters)
metropole.historicalNotes: Named for the Hotel Metropole—cognac and dry vermouth with a touch of syrup bridge Manhattan and Martini camps.
metropole.funFact: Hotel Metropole guests drank cognac like Americans drank rye—this spec splits the difference with dry vermouth.
metropole.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

opera.sourceRecipe: Savoy Opera (gin, maraschino, cream, orange bitters)
opera.historicalNotes: A dessert-leaning gin cocktail with cream and maraschino—named for London's theatrical district.
opera.funFact: Maraschino and cream with gin drinks like a cherry trifle—Craddock filed it under opera-house intermission sippers.
opera.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

poets-dream.historicalNotes: Split vermouths and absinthe surround gin—a fin-de-siècle flavor profile Craddock labeled for literary bohemians.
poets-dream.funFact: Absinthe rinse energy without the rinse—Poet's Dream keeps the herbaceous note in the stirred mix.
poets-dream.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

port-flip.historicalNotes: Ruby port substitutes for spirit in the flip template—Victorian after-dinner richness.
port-flip.funFact: Port flips trade spirit heat for wine sweetness—Thomas treated them as dessert in a coupe.
port-flip.sourceAttribution: How to Mix Drinks — Jerry Thomas

princeton.sourceRecipe: Savoy Princeton (old tom gin, port, orange bitters)
princeton.historicalNotes: Old tom gin's sweetness meets ruby port—named for the New Jersey university like many Ivy-themed Craddock drinks.
princeton.funFact: Old tom gin makes the Princeton sweeter than a dry-gin port split—Craddock assumed richer gin stock.
princeton.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

tipperary-cocktail.sourceRecipe: Savoy Tipperary (Irish whiskey, sweet vermouth, green Chartreuse)
tipperary-cocktail.historicalNotes: Irish whiskey Manhattan with Chartreuse—named for the Irish county during political ferment of the 1920s.
tipperary-cocktail.funFact: Green Chartreuse turns an Irish whiskey Manhattan into something herbal enough to split a room of purists.
tipperary-cocktail.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

hemingway-special.sourceRecipe: Hemingway Special / Papa Doble (rum, maraschino, grapefruit, lime, no sugar)
hemingway-special.recipeProvenance: Floridita house spec for Ernest Hemingway.
hemingway-special.historicalNotes: Ribalaigua tailored a sugarless daiquiri double for Hemingway—grapefruit and maraschino replace simple syrup.
hemingway-special.creator: Constantino Ribalaigua Vert
hemingway-special.funFact: Hemingway's diabetes drove the sugarless double—Floridita staff called it the Papa Doble before the IBA renamed it Hemingway Special.
hemingway-special.sourceAttribution: El Floridita / IBA lineage — Constantino Ribalaigua Vert

periodista.recipeProvenance: Journalists' bar template in Mexican cocktail literature.
periodista.historicalNotes: Tequila, coffee liqueur, and lime—a bitter-edged highball associated with Mexico City press rooms.
periodista.funFact: Periodista translates to journalist—Mexico City's reporters reportedly ordered tequila and coffee liqueur with lime after deadline.
periodista.sourceAttribution: Mexican bar canon — Documented Mexico City recipe

milk-punch.historicalNotes: Milk clarifies when acid curdles casein—Thomas documented the brandy template that Southern hosts bottled for holidays.
milk-punch.funFact: Clarified milk punch can sit bottled for months—the curdled milk strains out leaving silky brandy and spice.
milk-punch.sourceAttribution: How to Mix Drinks — Jerry Thomas

queens.sourceRecipe: Savoy Queen's (gin, ruby port, lemon, raspberry)
queens.historicalNotes: Gin and port split base with raspberry cordial—Craddock's royal naming convention for split-base sours.
queens.funFact: Ruby port and gin with raspberry reads like a British summer pudding turned cocktail.
queens.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

rose-cocktail.sourceRecipe: IBA Rose (dry vermouth, kirsch, raspberry syrup)
rose-cocktail.historicalNotes: Kirschwasser and dry vermouth with raspberry—distinct from the gin-based Rose cocktail slug elsewhere in this batch.
rose-cocktail.funFact: The IBA Rose is vermouth-forward with cherry eau-de-vie—no gin despite the delicate pink name.
rose-cocktail.sourceAttribution: IBA Official Cocktails — International Bartenders Association

star-cocktail.historicalNotes: Apple brandy Manhattan—American applejack culture filtered through London hotel bars.
star-cocktail.funFact: Two ingredients, equal parts—apple brandy and sweet vermouth drinks like a autumn Manhattan.
star-cocktail.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

imperial-fizz.sourceRecipe: Savoy Imperial Fizz (gin, lemon, egg white, champagne)
imperial-fizz.historicalNotes: Champagne tops a gin fizz—Imperial signaling the sparkling crown on a standard sour fizz.
imperial-fizz.funFact: Skip the soda in a gin fizz and top with champagne instead—you get the Imperial template Craddock printed.
imperial-fizz.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

nightcap.sourceRecipe: Savoy Nightcap (cognac, white crème de cacao, cream)
nightcap.historicalNotes: After-dinner wind-down—cognac and white cacao with cream in a small chilled format.
nightcap.funFact: Craddock's Nightcap predates the Golden Cadillac—cognac instead of Galliano for a quieter bedtime sip.
nightcap.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

king-cole.recipeProvenance: Berry reconstruction; grenadine and passion fruit stand in for fassionola.
king-cole.historicalNotes: Don the Beachcomber's King Cole used house fassionola—modern builds split grenadine and passion fruit syrup.
king-cole.funFact: Fassionola syrup vanished from production—today's King Cole rebuilds the red tropical note with grenadine and passion fruit.

man-o-war.sourceRecipe: Savoy Man O' War (bourbon, sweet vermouth, lemon, grenadine)
man-o-war.historicalNotes: Named for the WWI naval slogan—bourbon Manhattan with lemon and grenadine for a sour tilt.
man-o-war.funFact: Craddock named this for the Great War recruitment poster—bourbon and vermouth with a sour's citrus.
man-o-war.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

royal-hawaiian.sourceRecipe: Savoy Royal Hawaiian (gin, pineapple, lemon, orgeat)
royal-hawaiian.historicalNotes: Pre-tiki hotel drink—gin with pineapple and orgeat anticipates later Polynesian pop culture cocktails.
royal-hawaiian.funFact: Gin and orgeat rarely meet outside this spec—pineapple bridges the almond sweetness before tiki took over.
royal-hawaiian.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

san-francisco.sourceRecipe: San Francisco (crème de banane, vodka, pineapple, cream)
san-francisco.historicalNotes: Banana liqueur and cream define a 1970s dessert cocktail named for the California city.
san-francisco.funFact: Banana liqueur plus cream reads like a liquid dessert—Waldorf-era specs lean heavily on crème de banane.
san-francisco.sourceAttribution: The Old Waldorf-Astoria Bar Book — Albert Stevens Crockett

left-bank.historicalNotes: Elderflower liqueur and crisp white wine soften gin—a Lower East Side neo-speakeasy staple.
left-bank.funFact: Death & Co cut gin with Sauvignon Blanc and elderflower—Lower East Side drinkers called it the Left Bank.
left-bank.sourceAttribution: Death & Co — David Kaplan et al.

london-sour.sourceRecipe: Savoy London Sour (gin, lemon, triple sec, red wine float)
london-sour.historicalNotes: New York Sour's cousin with gin—lemon sour topped with a red wine float for color and tannin.
london-sour.funFact: Float claret on a gin sour and Craddock called it London—tannin on citrus without changing the base spirit.
london-sour.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

luau-grog.historicalNotes: Multi-rum grog with tropical citrus—luau service format from mid-century Hawaiian hospitality.
luau-grog.funFact: Luau grogs batch rum for crowds—Smuggler's Cove scales the spec for home mugs without losing spice.
luau-grog.sourceAttribution: Smuggler's Cove — Martin Cate & Rebecca Cate

honolulu-cooler.sourceRecipe: Savoy Honolulu Cooler (gin, pineapple, lemon, soda)
honolulu-cooler.historicalNotes: Gin cooler with pineapple and lemon—pre-tiki Hawaiian hotel bar template.
honolulu-cooler.funFact: Craddock printed Honolulu Cooler before Donn Beach imported Polynesian kitsch—gin and pineapple, not rum.
honolulu-cooler.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

havana-cooler.sourceRecipe: Savoy Havana Cooler (rum, lime, mint, soda)
havana-cooler.historicalNotes: Rum mojito-adjacent cooler with soda—Cuban template via London hotel printing.
havana-cooler.funFact: Mint, lime, rum, and soda in a Collins—Craddock's Havana Cooler predates the mojito's global fame.
havana-cooler.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

martinique-sour.sourceRecipe: Martinique Sour (rhum agricole, lime, orange curaçao, orgeat)
martinique-sour.historicalNotes: Rhum agricole sour with orgeat—Martinique's answer to the daiquiri with almond sweetness.
martinique-sour.funFact: Agricole rum's grassy funk needs orgeat to round the edges—Martinique bars treat this as the house sour.
martinique-sour.sourceAttribution: Smuggler's Cove — Martin Cate & Rebecca Cate

park-avenue.sourceRecipe: Savoy Park Avenue (gin, pineapple, sweet vermouth, orange juice)
park-avenue.historicalNotes: Manhattan-adjacent gin cocktail with pineapple—named for New York's luxury corridor.
park-avenue.funFact: Sweet vermouth and pineapple in a gin base drinks like a Waldorf hotel lounge special.
park-avenue.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

prohibition-punch.sourceRecipe: Savoy Prohibition Punch (gin, lemon, grenadine, egg white)
prohibition-punch.historicalNotes: Egg-white gin punch from the dry years—ironic naming as American Prohibition ended abroad.
prohibition-punch.funFact: Craddock labeled this Prohibition Punch while London never went dry—the name sold newspapers.
prohibition-punch.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

violet-fizz.sourceRecipe: Savoy Violet Fizz (gin, crème de violette, lemon, egg white, soda)
violet-fizz.historicalNotes: Crème de violette tints a gin fizz lavender—floral fizz family alongside the Aviation.
violet-fizz.funFact: Violet liqueur foams pink-purple under egg white—Craddock's floral answer to the Gin Fizz.
violet-fizz.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

viking-fizz.sourceRecipe: Savoy Viking Fizz (aquavit, lemon, egg white, soda)
viking-fizz.historicalNotes: Scandinavian spirit in a fizz template—caraway notes through citrus and foam.
viking-fizz.funFact: Aquavit's caraway in a fizz reads like rye bread meets lemon meringue—Craddock's Nordic nod.
viking-fizz.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

white-sangria.sourceRecipe: White sangria (white wine, brandy, citrus, soda)
white-sangria.historicalNotes: White wine sangria with brandy and seasonal fruit—lighter cousin to red sangria already in canon.
white-sangria.funFact: White sangria trades tannin for acidity—brandy and orange still anchor the punch bowl.
white-sangria.sourceAttribution: Spanish sangria tradition — Regional house format

polynesian-paralysis.historicalNotes: Rum and gin share a tiki mug—orgeat and lime tie the spirits together in 1960s Polynesian pop style.
polynesian-paralysis.funFact: Gin in a tiki mug sounds wrong until orgeat and three rums show up—Polynesian Paralysis lives up to its name.

apple-car.historicalNotes: Applejack sour with grenadine—American apple spirit in a British bar book.
apple-car.funFact: Applejack and grenadine make a pink sour without gin—Craddock filed it under whimsical fruit names.
apple-car.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

autumn-leaves.sourceRecipe: Savoy Autumn Leaves (rye, vermouth, apricot, bitters)
autumn-leaves.historicalNotes: Seasonal rye and vermouth with apricot brandy—Craddock's autumnal Manhattan variant.
autumn-leaves.funFact: Apricot brandy in a rye Manhattan reads like fall orchard—Craddock named it for foliage, not fashion.
autumn-leaves.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

beachcomber.sourceRecipe: Beachcomber (rum, triple sec, lime, Pernod substitute absinthe)
beachcomber.historicalNotes: Don the Beachcomber's early rum sour with anise—precursor DNA to later tiki complexity.
beachcomber.funFact: The Beachcomber is Donn Beach before the mugs got monstrous—rum, curaçao, lime, and a whisper of anise.

blackthorn.historicalNotes: Sloe gin and dry vermouth stirred—English hedgerow fruit in a low-ABV aperitif.
blackthorn.funFact: Sloe gin's plum tartness against dry vermouth drinks like a British countryside aperitivo.
blackthorn.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

charlie-chaplin.sourceRecipe: Savoy Charlie Chaplin (sloe gin, apricot, lime)
charlie-chaplin.historicalNotes: Named for the silent-film star—sloe gin and apricot liqueur with lime in a balanced sour.
charlie-chaplin.funFact: Craddock named this for Chaplin while the actor was London's biggest draw—sloe gin gives the sour a plum spine.
charlie-chaplin.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

don-the-beachcomber.recipeProvenance: Berry reconstruction of early Donn spec.
don-the-beachcomber.historicalNotes: Separate from dons-beachcomber in expanded set—this slug marks the classic named house cocktail format.
don-the-beachcomber.creator: Donn Beach
don-the-beachcomber.funFact: Berry distinguishes Don the Beachcomber the drink from Don the Beachcomber the bar—same owner, different recipe log.

hawaiian-eye.sourceRecipe: Savoy Hawaiian Eye (rum, gin, vermouth, citrus)
hawaiian-eye.historicalNotes: Split-spirit sour with vermouth—tiki-era naming before rum took over Hawaiian-themed drinks.
hawaiian-eye.funFact: Gin and rum in one glass was Craddock's idea of exotic—vermouth keeps the Hawaiian Eye from becoming chaos.
hawaiian-eye.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

torpedo.sourceRecipe: Savoy Torpedo (gin, sweet vermouth, absinthe, bitters)
torpedo.historicalNotes: Sweet vermouth-heavy gin stir with absinthe—naval naming in Craddock's metaphor-heavy index.
torpedo.funFact: Craddock's Torpedo loads absinthe into a sweet vermouth Martini—one of the Savoy's more aggressive stirs.
torpedo.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

jamaican-mule.sourceRecipe: Jamaican Mule (Jamaican rum, lime, ginger beer)
jamaican-mule.recipeProvenance: Moscow Mule variant with pot-still rum.
jamaican-mule.historicalNotes: Ginger beer and lime with funky Jamaican rum—the mule template applied to Caribbean spirit.
jamaican-mule.funFact: Swap vodka for Jamaican rum in a mule and the ginger beer suddenly tastes like Kingston.
jamaican-mule.sourceAttribution: Modern mule family — Documented bar template

kansas-city-ice-water.sourceRecipe: Savoy Kansas City Ice Water (rye, vermouth, absinthe, bitters)
kansas-city-ice-water.historicalNotes: High-proof stirred rye with absinthe rinse character—despite the name, served neat in a coupe.
kansas-city-ice-water.funFact: Ice Water on the label but no soda in the spec—Craddock meant the drink hits like cold water on a Kansas summer.
kansas-city-ice-water.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

knickerbocker.historicalNotes: New York Knickerbocker name—rum, raspberry, and citrus in an early American punch template.
knickerbocker.funFact: Thomas's Knickerbocker predates the frozen blender version—raspberry and rum in a wine-glass punch.
knickerbocker.sourceAttribution: How to Mix Drinks — Jerry Thomas

lawrence-of-arabia.sourceRecipe: Savoy Lawrence of Arabia (gin, brandy, citrus)
lawrence-of-arabia.historicalNotes: Named during T.E. Lawrence fever—split gin and brandy with lemon in a colonial-era sour.
lawrence-of-arabia.funFact: Craddock printed this as Lawrence of Arabia hit cinemas—gin and brandy share equal billing.
lawrence-of-arabia.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

mojito-cubano.sourceRecipe: Mojito Cubano (rum, mint, lime, sugar, soda)
mojito-cubano.recipeProvenance: Classic Cuban highball; distinct slug from house mojito.
mojito-cubano.historicalNotes: Explicit Cuban formatting—aguardiente-era rum, muddled mint, and cracked ice service.
mojito-cubano.funFact: La Bodeguita del Medio wrote mojito on the wall—this slug marks the Cuban service spec, not every house mojito.

port-o-call.sourceRecipe: Port O' Call (rum, port, lime, falernum)
port-o-call.historicalNotes: Ruby port and rum with falernum—maritime naming for a fortified-wine tiki hybrid.
port-o-call.funFact: Port in tiki sounds like a mistake until falernum and lime tie the wine to the rum base.
port-o-call.sourceAttribution: Smuggler's Cove — Martin Cate & Rebecca Cate

rose.sourceRecipe: IBA Rose (dry vermouth, kirsch, raspberry syrup)
rose.historicalNotes: Kirschwasser and dry vermouth—distinct from the stirred Rose Cocktail slug in this same batch.
rose.funFact: The IBA Rose is three ingredients and all vermouth-forward—cherry eau-de-vie does the aromatic work.
rose.sourceAttribution: IBA Official Cocktails — International Bartenders Association

yacht-club.sourceRecipe: Savoy Yacht Club (rum, dry vermouth, lime, bitters)
yacht-club.historicalNotes: Rum and dry vermouth with lime—yacht-club naming for a low-proof tropical Martini.
yacht-club.funFact: Dry vermouth and rum with lime drinks like a sailor's Martini—Craddock filed it under club life.
yacht-club.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

sbagliato.sourceRecipe: IBA Negroni Sbagliato (prosecco, Campari, sweet vermouth)
sbagliato.historicalNotes: Accounts credit a mistaken prosecco pour at Bar Basso in Milan—the 'wrong' Negroni became its own aperitivo staple.
sbagliato.funFact: Sbagliato means 'mistaken' in Italian—prosecco swapped in for gin and the accident stuck on menus worldwide.
sbagliato.sourceAttribution: IBA Official Cocktails — International Bartenders Association

dry-martini.recipeProvenance: IBA Unforgettables — 6:1 gin to vermouth build.
dry-martini.historicalNotes: The dry Martini is its own branch of bartending argument—ratio, gin choice, and olive versus twist.
dry-martini.funFact: The IBA spec keeps the pour gin-forward—six parts gin to one part dry vermouth, stirred and icy.
dry-martini.sourceAttribution: IBA Official Cocktails — International Bartenders Association

mermaid.historicalNotes: Split rum and gin tiki sour—Mermaid naming in Polynesian pop menus of the 1960s.
mermaid.funFact: The Mermaid hides gin inside a rum sour—falernum makes the split spirits taste like one tropical voice.

imperial-cocktail.sourceRecipe: Savoy Imperial Cocktail (gin, maraschino, apricot, lime)
imperial-cocktail.historicalNotes: Imperial naming for a gin sour with stone-fruit liqueurs—distinct from the Imperial Fizz in this batch.
imperial-cocktail.funFact: Craddock used Imperial for both fizz and this gin sour—check the slug before you grab egg white or champagne.
imperial-cocktail.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

japanese-slipper.recipeProvenance: Later popularized; Savoy-adjacent modern classic documented in secondary sources.
japanese-slipper.historicalNotes: Melon liqueur, triple sec, and lemon—a 1980s international bar staple attributed to Australian service.
japanese-slipper.funFact: Japanese Slipper landed in Australian bars in the 1980s—green melon liqueur made it impossible to miss on a menu.
japanese-slipper.sourceAttribution: The Savoy Cocktail Book — Harry Craddock

london-fog.sourceRecipe: London Fog (gin, earl grey, vanilla, cream)
london-fog.recipeProvenance: Modern tea cocktail; gin base variant.
london-fog.historicalNotes: Earl grey and cream with gin—a cocktail riff on the non-alcoholic London Fog latte template.
london-fog.funFact: The boozy London Fog swaps tea latte comfort for gin—bergamot and cream still do the heavy lifting.
london-fog.sourceAttribution: Cafe culture template — Documented tea-cocktail format

mimosa.historicalNotes: Champagne and orange at equal parts—1920s Paris hotel brunch staple.
mimosa.funFact: The Mimosa is half juice, half bubbles—Paris hotel bars needed a morning drink lighter than a Buck's Fizz.
